growth_story.headline: Italy's income per person fell through two crises after 2007 and is only now about back to that level, with growth held down by weak productivity and ageing.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2006 income per person grew 1.3 percent a year, while the IMF found that productivity had stopped rising from the late 1990s. From 2007 to 2014 it shrank 1.3 percent a year, with a fall of 5.9 percent in 2009 in the global financial crisis. Then the euro area debt crisis brought a second recession, with falls of 3.4 percent in 2012 and 2.0 percent in 2013, as confidence fell, credit tightened and banks' bad loans piled up. Since 2015 growth has again averaged 1.3 percent a year, but the era holds a pandemic fall of 8.4 percent in 2020 and a rebound of 9.5 percent in 2021 and 5.0 percent in 2022, led by services, tourism and construction backed by tax credits. Growth then eased to 1.0 percent in 2023, 0.8 in 2024 and 0.6 in 2025, with investment under the EU-funded recovery plan helping to hold it up. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, but that is about where it first stood in 2007, and over 2006–2015 it fell 0.8 percent a year before rising 1.3 percent a year over 2016–2025.

threads.title: Productivity stalled for decades
threads.text: The IMF traces Italy's slow growth to productivity that has barely risen since the late 1990s. It links this to a hard business climate, a split labor market and little competition in services. Its 2026 report says Italy is still caught in a cycle of low productivity and low growth.

threads.title: Two crises, one long slump
threads.text: From the middle of 2011 the euro area debt crisis pushed Italy into a second recession as confidence fell and credit tightened. Loan losses then hurt banks' profits and slowed the recovery, so output did not pass its level from before the global financial crisis until 2024.

threads.title: Pandemic rebound and recovery plan
threads.text: After the 2020 fall, services, tourism and building work boosted by home-renovation tax credits drove a quick rebound. As those tax credits were cut back, investment under the EU-funded National Recovery and Resilience Plan became a main support for growth.

threads.title: A shrinking, ageing workforce
threads.text: Births have fallen for decades and dropped sharply after the global financial crisis, so the number of people of working age has been falling. The IMF expects this, together with weak productivity, to keep growth slow over the medium term.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 0.6 percent in 2025, the slowest of the last three years, while employment stayed near record highs. In 2026 a war in the Middle East pushed up world energy prices. The IMF's July 2026 report says inflation picked up because Italy relies on imported fuel, and it expects growth to stay slow.

citations.quote: the recent surge in global energy prices following the war in the Middle East has put economic growth in jeopardy

citations.quote: Amid the increase in global energy prices, domestic inflation has picked up, reflecting Italy's dependence on imported fossil fuels.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person at its highest level yet in 2025, and the latest era (2015–2025) growing 1.3 percent a year, as fast as 1990–2006. The IMF instead describes a modest pace below the euro area average. The gap narrows on a closer look. The era average is lifted by the 9.5 percent rebound in 2021 after the 8.4 percent fall in 2020. Yearly growth since 2023 has been 1.0 percent or less. And the 2025 peak is only about the level first reached in 2007, so the record mostly marks lost ground won back, not fast growth.
